rawItems.title: Crews rush to 'deliberate' fire at former RAF base in Hunts village
rawItems.content: Firefighters rushed to a "deliberate" fire at a derelict former RAF base in a Huntingdonshire village. Crews were called to the former RAF Upwood site on Ramsey Road near Bury on Saturday, November 21, at 3.31pm. The base opened in 1917 after a nearby farm was requisitioned for use as an emergency landing ground. Standing mostly derelict since 1994, the site has been the target of fly tipping and arson attacks for a number of years. However, there have been plans to redevelop areas into community facilities. Crews from Ramsey arrived to find a blaze on the ground floor of the derelict building and used a hose reel to extinguish it. They returned to the station by 4.10pm. A statement from Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service reads: "The cause of the fire is believed to be deliberate." Anyone with information should contact Cambridgeshire Police via their website, quoting incident 445 of November 21. Alternatively, call Crimestoppers on 0800 555111.

rawItems.title: New café and bistro on the cards for Huntingdonshire town
rawItems.content: A new café and bistro could be on the cards for Ramsey if plans are approved. Turquazze Restaurant Ltd has submitted a fresh premises licence application to Huntingdonshire District Council. Bloom and Brew would operate from the unit previously occupied by Konak Café and Grill, on 34 Great Whyte. According to the applicant, the bistro would serve breakfast, lunch and dinner, including British and Mediterranean cuisine. "The premises has approximately 70 customer seats. Alcohol will be served indoors only, with meals, by waiter service at tables. "No off-sales of alcohol are proposed," the plans said. "Bloom and Brew will operate as a family-friendly café and restaurant. "Alcohol will only be served with meals, by waiter service at tables, staff will be trained in responsible alcohol sales, public safety and child protection. "The premises will be properly managed and supervised." If approved, the venue would serve alcohol for consumption on the premises between the hours of 8am and 10.30pm Monday to Sunday. Members of the public can make representations concerning the application, either in writing or by email to licensing@huntingdonshire.gov.uk. To have your say on the application visit the district council's public register by no later than November 26. Have you got a story you want to share? rawItems.title: 9 hidden gems in Cambridgeshire you have to visit at least once
rawItems.content: Cambridgeshire is packed with hidden gems that rarely make the county's tourism brochures. From ancient wetlands and secret nature reserves to forgotten archaeological sites and historic country estates, here are nine lesser-known attractions to visit. Often described as a hidden gem, Wicken Fen is the National Trust's oldest nature reserve and one of Europe's most important wetlands. Visitors can explore boardwalks winding through reedbeds, marshes and wildflower meadows while spotting dragonflies, rare birds and grazing Highland cattle. The reserve offers a glimpse into the ancient Fenland landscape that once dominated the region, making it an excellent destination for walkers, families and wildlife enthusiasts. Hidden away between Peterborough and Huntingdon, Holme Fen feels remarkably wild and remote. The reserve is home to the famous Holme Post, marking Britain's lowest land point at around 2.75 metres below sea level. Visitors can explore peaceful woodland trails, wetlands and bird hides while discovering a fascinating story of how drainage transformed the Fens. One of Britain's last remaining washlands, Nene Washes offers spectacular wildlife viewing throughout the year. Winter floods attract thousands of migratory birds, while spring and summer bring breeding cranes, godwits and marsh harriers. Birdwatchers rate it among the county's finest locations, yet it remains surprisingly under the radar with many local visitors. Covering hundreds of acres beside the River Nene
